title: Knowledge Check 6: Lessons 26-30
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 26-30 of the ai-power-user series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Priya has four working workflows and wants her fifth to take a fraction of the time her first did. Per the lesson, what is the turning point that makes her fifth workflow cheap to build?
options: She memorizes the details of each workflow so she can rebuild them from memory faster
She extracts the general, proven pieces from her finished workflows into a reusable library she can assemble new workflows from
She works on one workflow each day so her speed improves through repetition
She copies the same prompt into every new workflow to make sure nothing is lost
questions.explanation: The lesson's whole point is that the fifth workflow is cheap because by then Priya reaches for saved templates, shared house-style instructions, structured-output contracts, and tested connectors from her library, so she does not solve those problems again. Memorizing, daily repetition, or copy-pasting the same prompt into everything describe duplication, the opposite of the compounding the lesson teaches.

questions.question: Priya finds she has written four slightly different versions of her house-style voice and tone rules, one at the start of each workflow. Per the lesson, what is the correct move?
options: Keep all four so each workflow always has its own personal copy
Merge them into one authoritative house-style instruction that every workflow references instead of carrying its own
Delete the instructions entirely so the tool writes in whatever tone it wants
Write a fifth, longer version and add it to every workflow
questions.explanation: The lesson applies the DRY principle here: keeping one authoritative copy of each piece of knowledge, referenced everywhere, is the discipline that stops libraries from rotting, because one edit fixes the style everywhere instead of four. Keeping four copies, deleting them, or adding a fifth longer one all describe duplication the lesson explicitly warns against.

questions.question: You are deciding whether a saved prompt belongs in your automation library. Per the lesson, which piece passes the tests for a building block?
options: A prompt with a specific client's name and their exact approval phrasing baked in, used by that one workflow
A connector you have configured but never actually run in any workflow
A parameterized template with clearly marked slots that serves more than one workflow and was proven by a working run
A draft house-style rule you intended to follow but have not yet used
questions.explanation: The lesson gives three tests: generality (serves more than one workflow), proven (from a workflow that works, not a guess), and findable. A parameterized template that serves many workflows and was proven by a working run passes all three. The client-specific prompt is a one-off, and the unused connector and unused draft rule fail the proven test.

questions.question: Per the lesson, which of the five selection tests is the capstone-specific one that a one-prompt job fails?
options: It is medium: three to six connected steps with a real input contract, an output contract, and a human review gate, not a one-prompt job
It is real: a task you actually run at least monthly
It is same-shaped: the same inputs, steps, and output format every time
It is worth the build: the setup pays back on a real schedule
questions.explanation: The lesson calls test four, the medium test, the capstone-specific one. A one-prompt job has one step and no assembly, so it fails it: there is nothing to assemble and you will not practice the pattern.

questions.question: According to the lesson, what is the definition of done for a workflow?
options: The checklist a completed run must pass, which is the finish line Capstone B builds against
The list of tools the workflow uses
The schedule that triggers each run
The list of tasks that are explicitly out of scope
questions.explanation: The lesson defines the definition of done as the checklist a run must pass before you trust it, and says it is the finish line Capstone B needs and the quality bar you set in Lesson 18.

questions.question: In Priya's scope, which section catches the silent failure where a flagged vendor is dropped from the digest?
options: The definition of done, because it includes a row-count check that the flagged rows in the digest equal the count in the source
The boundaries section, because it lists what is out of scope
The trigger section, because it names when the run starts
The one-sentence job, because it states what the workflow does
questions.explanation: The lesson maps each silent failure to a check in the definition of done. A dropped flag dies on the row-count check, which requires the flagged rows in the digest to equal the count in the source.

questions.question: Per the lesson, when you design the pipeline from your scope, what is the right way to catch wiring mistakes before you connect anything?
options: Write down each step's input, action, and output in order, and fix any step whose output does not cleanly match the next step's input
Build all the steps first and run them together to see what breaks
Add error handling to every step before the first full run
Wire in the calendar trigger so real runs happen on schedule
questions.explanation: The lesson's design pass has you write the input, action, and output for each step in order. Because one step's output is the next step's input, writing them together is how you catch mismatches cheaply, before you wire anything.

questions.question: What is assembly, as the lesson defines it, and why is it faster and more reliable than authoring?
options: Putting an automation together from library pieces that already exist and are known to fit, which is faster and more reliable because every reused piece is already tested
Writing each piece fresh so the workflow is fully original
Copying an existing workflow and changing the names
Building one connected tool at a time from scratch
questions.explanation: Assembly means wiring reusable pieces from the library into the workflow instead of re-authoring them. Reusing a piece is reusing something already tested, which is why assembly is faster and more reliable.

questions.question: In Priya's dry run, what was the first-run failure and how did she fix it?
options: The deliver step gave the dated filename the input folder's last-modified date instead of the current month; she fixed it with a one-line change in the deliver step's instruction and re-ran
The draft step could not read the normalized table, so she rewrote the template from scratch
The normalize step dropped every flagged vendor, so she re-authored the connector
The review gate was skipped, so she removed it from the workflow
questions.explanation: Priya's first dry run failed because the deliver step dated the filename from the input folder rather than the run date. It was a one-line fix in the deliver step's instruction, and the second dry run passed every check in her definition of done.

questions.question: A workflow has a review step that says the owner 'reads the draft before it goes out.' Which change turns that habit into a gate, as the lesson defines it?
options: Name the specific checks, block the deliver step when any check fails, record the decision in the run log, and give the review a due time
Add a second person to read the draft as well
Add a reminder message that fires on the morning the digest is due
Move the review step earlier so there is more time to fix problems
questions.explanation: The lesson gives four tests for a gate: it names the check, it has a stop condition so delivery cannot proceed on failure, it records the decision, and it has an owner and a due time with a stale-review alarm. A reminder or a second reader leaves delivery unblocked.

questions.question: In Priya's edge-case test, the missing-file folder passed validation when it should have failed. What was the cause and the fix?
options: Validate counted files in the folder, and a leftover prior-month file made the count look complete; she changed it to match filenames against the expected month pattern
The normalize step silently dropped the missing file; she added a dedupe key
The draft step produced an empty digest; she added an empty-state line
The deliver step wrote the file with the wrong date; she dated it from the run date
questions.explanation: Validate was checking the number of files present, and last month's export still in the folder satisfied that count. The fix was to validate filenames against the expected month pattern rather than counting whatever the folder contained.

questions.question: Which measure specifically converts a silent failure (a run that reports success while the output is wrong) into a loud one?
options: A post-run check that reconciles the flagged count in the output against the count in the source, and fails the run when they disagree
A longer retry policy so a failing step gets more attempts
A more detailed prompt so the drafting step is less likely to make mistakes
A canary period where the output goes to you before it goes to the audience
questions.explanation: The lesson names count reconciliation, field presence, and expected-content checks as the post-run checks that catch quiet failures. A canary limits blast radius and retries help recovery, but neither detects that the output itself is wrong.

questions.question: A colleague who has never seen your workflow tries to run one cycle using only your runbook entry, and stops at the inputs section asking which of two similarly named folders is authoritative. What does the lesson say this outcome means?
options: The handover test worked: the stop is a missing field, and the input section needs the exact path and naming pattern written down
The colleague lacks prerequisite expertise, so the entry is complete and the failure is on their side
The runbook entry is too long and should be cut back to the ordered steps only
The workflow should be retired, because a confusing input location means the pipeline is unreliable
questions.explanation: The lesson defines the handover test as giving the entry to someone who has never run the workflow and watching where they stop, and states that every stop is a missing field. Priya's own test surfaced exactly this ambiguity about two folders with similar names.

questions.question: You are writing a decision record for choosing a monthly rather than weekly cadence. Which element does the lesson treat as the one that makes the record genuinely useful?
options: The condition under which you would reverse the decision, such as the input publishing weekly or a breach landing mid-month
A longer narrative explaining every option you considered and rejected in detail
An approval signature from a manager confirming the cadence was authorized
A screenshot of the scheduling configuration so the settings can be reproduced
questions.explanation: The lesson says the value sits in the third part of the record, what would change your mind, because a decision with no stated reversal condition can only be argued about rather than revisited honestly. Length and screenshots are not part of the format it gives.

questions.question: Your retro numbers are 8 hours total to build and a net saving of 2.5 hours per month. Why does the lesson insist on reporting break-even rather than saying the workflow saves time?
options: Build cost divided by monthly return gives a break-even in months, which is a defensible claim, while saving time is not a claim anyone can check
Break-even is only needed when the workflow cost more to build than a month of the manual task
Break-even should be reported only after the workflow has run for a full year so the figure is final
The monthly return should always be rounded up to the nearest hour before dividing, to keep the number tidy
questions.explanation: The lesson states that build cost divided by monthly return is the break-even in months, and that reporting it is a defensible thing to say to a manager and a completely different sentence from saying the workflow saves time.
